## Introduction.

Magic was regarded by the ancients as the highest and holiest of all sciences, and among all peoples it was introduced and taught under the veil of the mysteries <note>The "Ancient Mysteries" were secret religious rites of the Greco-Roman world, such as those at Eleusis, which were open only to initiated individuals.</note>. According to the concepts of that time, it consisted of the knowledge of all visible and invisible forces of the universe, and their secret or manifest effects; it contained the explanation of all nature, the knowledge of the relationship of all things, as well as their mutual antipathies and sympathies <note>original: "Ab- und Zuneigung." In early modern science and magic, "sympathy" and "antipathy" were the natural forces of attraction and repulsion that explained how things interacted (e.g., a magnet and iron).</note> and the consequences arising therefrom.

It extended, therefore, over both the spiritual and the sensory domains. It was divided into the physical or natural, the mathematical or celestial <note>In this context, "mathematical" magic often refers to astrology, astronomy, and the study of planetary influences based on numerical ratios.</note>, and the theological or ceremonial branches. The physical part contained the teachings regarding the nature of everything that exists in the world—its causes, effects, timings, local circumstances, changes, and events, both in their entirety and in detail. The mathematical part explained the

But when, after the emergence of Christianity, people began to merge pagan philosophy with Christian religious concepts and to establish the so-called Neoplatonic system, everything sank back once more into the darkness of the past. The pure and simple teaching of Christ was disfigured by superstition and fanaticism <note>The original German *Schwärmerey* refers to a state of excessive, often delusional religious enthusiasm or "wild-eyed" devotion.</note>; ceremony displaced the religion of the heart everywhere. People were no longer satisfied with brightening their prospects for a future life through blameless, pure morals and active love for their fellow man; they wanted to explore the future through all sorts of superstitious means and ceremonies. Fortune-telling, witchcraft, necromancy <note>The practice of communicating with the spirits of the dead to predict the future.</note>, the doctrine of a universal medicine <term>Universal medicine: also known as a panacea, a mythical substance or "elixir of life" supposed to cure all ailments.</term>, of the philosopher’s stone, of sympathy and antipathy <note>In early modern thought, "sympathy and antipathy" were occult forces believed to cause natural attractions and repulsions between substances, plants, or animals.</note>, and all the nonsense of ancient times were unearthed again and turned into articles of faith. Following them, others stepped onto the path that had been cleared and gradually expanded the domain of human knowledge through their discoveries. ...and writings, which in recent times are distributed both secretly and publicly, and where each one always seeks to surpass the other in obscure presentation and mystical explanations, I came upon the idea to summarize the actual system of ancient <term>Magic</term> <note>In this context, "Magic" refers to a formal system of esoteric knowledge rather than simple superstition.</note>, as it is scattered throughout many old and rare writings, into a brief extract and to publish it. The <term>Materialist</term> <note>Someone who believes that only physical matter exists, denying the spiritual or supernatural.</note> will thus find a refutation of his system here just as little as the <term>Theosophist</term>, <term>Teacher of Spirits</term> <note>Original German: *Geisterlehrer*. ...and writings, which in recent times are distributed both secretly and publicly, and where each one always seeks to surpass the other in obscure presentation and mystical explanations, I came upon the idea to summarize the actual system of ancient <term>Magic</term> <note>In this context, "Magic" refers to a formal system of esoteric knowledge and philosophy rather than simple superstition or stage magic.</note>, as it is scattered throughout many old and rare writings, into a brief extract and to publish it. This is intended to enable many an unbiased reader to judge these newer secret teachings with a proper knowledge of the subject, to separate the bad from the good, and to be able to survey the entire doctrine with an impartial eye.

The <term>Materialist</term> <note>A philosopher who believes that only physical matter exists, denying the existence of the soul or a spiritual realm.</note> will thus find a refutation of his system here just as little as the <term>Theosophist</term>, <term>Teacher of Spirits</term> <note>Original German: *Geisterlehrer*. This term likely refers to pneumatologists or individuals who claimed the ability to communicate with or categorize spiritual beings.</note>, and <term>Alchemist</term> may expect a defense of theirs. I shall present things as they were, and in part still are. I leave the judgment of these matters to the reader’s own discretion.

Written in September 1785.

->The Editor.<-

## Chapter One.

->§. 1.<-
->On the Elements.<-

All bodies in this <term>lower world<note>Referring to the "sublunary" realm in Aristotelian philosophy—the physical world below the moon which is subject to change and decay.</note></term> take their origin from the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. They arise not through a mere composition or accumulation of parts, but through the transformation of one into the other, and upon their destruction, they are dissolved back into the elements. None of these <term>sensible elements<note>Elements that can be perceived by the human senses, as opposed to "pure" philosophical elements.</note></term> is entirely pure; rather, they are more or less mixed, and one may be transformed into another. Thus, for example, pure earth—or <term>salt<note>In the alchemical tradition, "Salt" often represents the principle of solidity and the physical body.</note></term>—becomes water when in water; when thickened, it becomes earth again; driven upward by heat, it becomes air, and there, through further heating, it becomes fire. In the same way, it descends again step by step to earth, stone, <term>sulfur<note>In alchemy, "Sulfur" represents the principle of inflammability, oiliness, and the soul.</note></term>, and so forth. Each element has two essential qualities, one of which belongs to it alone, while the other is regarded as a <term>medium of union<note>A bridge or connecting principle; elements share one quality with their "neighboring" element, allowing for a natural transition between states.</note></term> with the following element. Thus, fire is warm and

<summary>This page introduces the fundamental alchemical and natural philosophical theory of the four elements, explaining how all matter originates from and dissolves back into fire, air, water, and earth through constant transformation.</summary>
<keywords>four elements, alchemy, transformation, sublunary world, salt, sulfur, essential qualities, natural philosophy</keywords>

### On the Magic of the Ancients.

dry, the earth cold and dry, water cold and moist, and air warm and moist. Therefore, the elements, according to their contrary qualities, are opposed to one another—just as water is to fire, and earth to air. Furthermore, they are opposed to one another in regard to their weight: water and earth, as the heavier ones, are opposed to air and fire, as the lighter ones. Therefore, the former are called <term>passive<note>From the Latin *patiens*, these are the elements that are acted upon or receive influence.</note></term>, and the latter are called <term>active<note>From the Latin *agens*, these elements provide the force or heat that initiates change.</note></term>. Moreover, Plato assigns three kinds of properties to each element: to fire, penetrability, fineness, and motion; but to earth, density, darkness, and rest. By virtue of these properties, fire is the opposite of earth. The remaining two elements take on some of these properties: air, for example, takes on two properties of fire—fineness and motion—and one from earth, namely darkness; conversely, water receives two properties from earth—darkness and density—and one from fire, namely motion. Fire is twice as fine, three times more mobile, and four times more penetrating than air; air, on the other hand, is twice as penetrating, three times finer, and four times more mobile than water; and water is twice as penetrating, three times finer, and four times more mobile than earth. Fire thus relates to air as air relates to water, and water to earth, and vice versa. This is the foundation of all corporeality, of all natures, powers, and wonderful properties. The ancients further divided the elements generally into three classes.

# Chapter One.

Classes. Those of the first class are completely pure, uncompounded, unchangeable, suffer no mixing, are indestructible, and through them all the powers of things obtain their reality. The elements of the second class are changeable, manifold, impure, and can be brought back to their original purity through <term>art<note>In this context, "Art" (German: *Kunst*) refers to alchemy or the technical application of hidden knowledge to refine and transform nature.</note></term>. Those of the third class are not actually elements in themselves; they are changeable, manifold, decomposed, and mutually transformable into one another; they are the actual so-called <term>middle beings<note>Original: *Mittelwesen*. These are transitional substances or forces that bridge the gap between the purely spiritual and the purely material realms.</note></term>, and are also called the middle nature. Their powers are less known, and yet all effects of natural and divine magic rely on this important knowledge, just as, in general, no magical effect can be produced without the science and insight of these three classes of elements.

->§. 2.<-

->On Fire and Earth.<-

Fire and earth, or the active and the passive, are sufficient for all natural effects. Fire is in everything, permeates and illuminates everything, and its origin is unknown and hidden. Without matter upon which it can manifest its effect, it is immeasurable and invisible; it has the ground of its effect within itself, is movable, intangible, and everywhere present; it suffers no loss and shares itself with everything. It is one, and as the <term>Pythagoreans<note>Followers of Pythagoras, the ancient Greek philosopher who believed the universe was structured according to mathematical ratios and that fire was a central cosmic principle.</note></term> claim, it is extended and radiant in the heavenly regions; in the

### On the Magic of the Ancients.

In the lowest regions, however, fire is compressed, agonizing, and dark; in the middle regions, on the other hand, it takes on a dual nature. It is present in stones, where it can be coaxed out with steel; in the earth, as can be seen in the vapors rising from it; in the water, it warms the springs and wells, and with the help of the winds, it removes the coldness from seawater; in the air, as is well known, it often stirs up the greatest storms, and everything that lives, lives through the fire dwelling within it. The upper fire possesses a warmth that makes all things fruitful and illuminates everything; the lower fire, by contrast, has a consuming heat and destroys all fertility. The Father of Light <note>A theological term for the Creator or the source of all spiritual and material illumination.</note> allows His rays to emanate from Himself, sharing them first with the sun and the other celestial bodies, and from there it descends to our fire, as if through channels. Just as the spirits of darkness are stronger and more powerful in the gloom, the good spirits rejoice not only in the divine, the solar, and the celestial light or fire, but also in our own. This is presumably the source of the custom of lighting lamps during all religious ceremonies. For this very reason, Pythagoras also said that one should not speak of God without light; and for this same reason, candles were lit beside the bodies of the deceased, because it was believed that evil spirits were driven away by them. In all the sacrifices of the ancients, fire had to be present; and the Romans kept it always burning upon the altar during the <term>Vestal service<note>The cult of the Roman goddess Vesta, where the "Vestal Virgins" maintained a sacred eternal flame representing the hearth of the city.</note></term>, imposing the harshest punishments if it should ever go out through carelessness.

* The absurdities of this doctrine are evident. For firstly, if dreams and other impressions depended on the air that currently surrounds me, no other idea could enter my soul than of things that are around me or have been spoken of; yet we know that one can dream of entirely foreign things that have probably never happened or been mentioned in the place where the dream occurs; indeed, one often dreams suddenly without any cause of things one has not thought of for years. Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the founder of Neoplatonism; he believed that all objects emit "species" or images of themselves.</note> claimed that certain not merely spiritual, but natural images of things emanate from them through a certain efflux, linger in the air, and then, through light or movement, reach our sight or other senses, where they can reveal and present themselves to us. When a south wind arises and the clouds are thinned, one sees—as if in a mirror—various figures of distant things, such as camps, mountains, horses, people, etc. ** which vanish again as the clouds part; likewise, in humid air, likenesses of things can be represented that are entirely similar to the things themselves. And Aristotle tells of a man whose eyesight was so weak that his eyes could not penetrate the air for more than a few steps. It served him, therefore, like a mirror, and presented him with his own likeness wherever he went or stood. ->§. 4.<-

### On the Properties of Composite Things, and How They Relate to the Elements.

Following the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> are the four perfect bodies composed of them. These are stones, metals, plants, and animals. While every element contributes its part to their production, each individual thing possesses more or less of one or another specific element. The stones are all earthy, heavy, incline toward the center of the earth, and possess such dryness that they are almost entirely infusible <term>infusible: unable to be melted or fused by heat</term>. The metals are of a watery nature, meltable, and are produced through a viscous moisture. The plants stand so much under the rule of the air that they can neither germinate nor grow without it. The same applies to animals; for fire is so indispensably necessary to them that with its cessation, life itself disappears simultaneously <note>In traditional natural philosophy, "fire" in animals refers to "innate heat," the biological warmth considered essential for life.</note>. These four types are further distinguished from one another according to the degrees of the elements: thus, among stones, those that are opaque and heavy are called earthy; those that are transparent and arise from water—such as crystal, beryl, shell pearls, and the like—are called watery; those are airy which on

Among **animals**, one may name as earthy the **worms**, **moles**, and other creeping creatures that dwell in the earth; **fish** are watery; others cannot live outside of the **air**; and still others are to be called fiery because they can endure within it, such as the **salamander** \*; furthermore, those that carry a fiery heat within them belong here, such as **pigeons**, **ostriches**, **lions**, and others. These latter fluids themselves are again divided according to the elements: **red bile** <note>Commonly referred to in the humoral system as yellow bile or choler.</note> belongs to fire, **blood** to air, **fat** to water, and **black bile** to earth. ## On the Magic of the Ancients.

...according to the testimony of **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD). This likely refers to his theories on the soul and sensory perception, which were frequently cited in later esoteric and natural philosophy to link the microcosm of man to the macrocosm of the elements.</note>, the **understanding** <note>original: "Verstand"; in this context, the analytic or intellectual faculty.</note> corresponds to **fire**, **reason** <note>original: "Vernunft"; the higher faculty of wisdom and logic.</note> to **air**, the **imagination** to **water**, and the **senses** to **earth**. Among these latter, the sense of **sight** belongs to fire, because nothing can be seen without fire or light; **hearing** is of an airy nature by virtue of sound; **smell** and **taste** belong to water, for without its influence neither one nor the other can arise; **touch** is entirely earthy. Finally, the actions and conduct of men can also be divided according to the elements; for a slow and composed demeanor bears witness to the **earth**; fear, sluggishness, and negligence to **water**; cheerfulness and pleasant behavior correspond with the **air**, while impetuous and angry conduct, on the other hand, corresponds with **fire**. Thus, the elements are the beginning of all things; from them and through them everything arises, and they are again contained in everything, communicating their powers to all beings.

->§. 5.<-

### Classification of the Elements according to Heaven, the Stars, Spirits, Angels, etc.

In the upper world, according to the unanimous opinion of the ancients, everything is constituted just as it is in this corporeal world, only modified in various ways depending on the nature of the receiving things. Thus, according to this teaching, the elements are to be found in this lower world as well as in heaven, in the stars, in the spirits, angels, and finally in the **Great Architect** <term>Great Architect: original "Werkmeister," a term referring to the divine creator or Demiurge who ordered the universe from chaos.</term> himself. ### §. 6.
### On the Elemental Forces of Things.

The natural elemental forces of things are divided into three orders. Those of the **first order** are warming, cooling, moistening, and drying; these four properties alone can change the entire substance of bodies, something which those of the second and third orders cannot do so easily. The forces of the **second order** arise from the mixing of the elements. Thus, for example, besides the first four indicated properties, some things are ripening <note>original: "zeitigend"; in early science, this refers to the process of maturing, digesting, or bringing a substance to its peak state</note>,

So, for example, **ripening** <term>Zeitigung: the process of bringing fruit, or a medical condition like an abscess, to maturity or a state of readiness</term> is an effect of heat according to a certain measure of material substance, whereas hardness is an effect of cold, etc. These powers, insofar as they act upon a specific limb—such as promoting urine, or stimulating milk and the **monthly cleansing** <note>original: "monatliche Reinigung"; a historical term for menstruation</note>—are counted as belonging to the **third order**; and by means of these three orders, a great many diseases are alleviated or cured. Many other powers are brought about through artifice: such as the so-called **Greek fire**, which burns in water; fire that is extinguished by oil and ignited by cold water; incombustible oils; and lamps that are extinguished by neither wind nor water, as is claimed of the one that burned in the Temple of Venus and was sustained by **asbestos stone** <term>asbestos: in ancient and medieval thought, asbestos was often considered a "mineral wool" that could serve as a perpetual wick for eternal lamps because it was not consumed by the flame</term>. To this category also belongs wood prepared in a certain way so that it is not consumed by fire, as well as the ointments with which one coats the hands to handle glowing iron unharmed or to dip one's fingers into liquid metal.

# Second Chapter.

### §. 1.

## Of the World Spirit.

Many of the ancient philosophers, among whom Orpheus, Pythagoras, and others are numbered, asserted that all of nature was full of gods. This can be explained quite naturally if one understands these "gods" to be the living forces of things, and assumes that God himself is the origin of all life and all power.

Many and various names were attributed to these forces. It is from this that it follows that they were later personified under the names of gods, and good and evil **demons** <note>original: "Dämonen"; in this historical context, the term refers to the Greek "daimon," a spirit or divine power that acts as an intermediary between gods and mortals, not necessarily an evil entity</note>; some called them souls or spirits because the powers of things depend upon them. For it is the nature of a spirit alone to extend itself from one substance over another and to work within it, just as a human being can extend their spirit toward spiritual things and their imagination toward imagined objects. And this was what was meant when the ancients said that the spirit of a thing leaves it, passes over to another, takes possession of it, and hinders or promotes its effect.

Now, since the soul is the first cause of motion—and is furthermore entirely free and contains the basis of motion within itself—while the body or matter, on the other hand, is completely inactive and too greatly opposed to the nature of the soul:

This power of attraction occurs through the influence of the **stars** <note>original: "Gestirne"</note>, insofar as they have some similarity or kinship with things.

For the less embodied it is, the greater is its effect, and the faster it reproduces its own kind. ### §. 2.
## Of the Secret Powers of Things.

All things possess, in addition to their elementary powers <term>elementary powers: properties arising from the four elements—earth, water, air, and fire—such as heat, cold, moisture, or dryness</term>, other more secret powers which depend on their form or essence. Because of this, it happens that a small quantity can sometimes produce great effects, which is not possible for purely elementary natures. These powers, which reside more within the essence itself, are therefore capable of achieving a great deal with very little matter; the elementary power, however, being material itself, also requires much matter to produce a significant effect. They are called "secret powers" <note>original: "geheime Kräfte"; often referred to in Latin as *virtutes occultae*, these are properties that cannot be explained by physical touch or temperature alone</note> because their causes are hidden, so that they cannot be entirely discovered, and have become known more through long experience than through sharp reflection. So, for example, we know that foods are digested by the heat of the stomach, but they are transformed [into nourishment] by another power unknown to us, and so forth. The ancients, and among them especially the *Platonists*, explained the origin of these powers as follows: All things of the lower world <note>the physical or "sublunary" realm we inhabit</note> arise through the *Ideas* of the upper world. These *Ideas* are incorporeal forms, souls, or minds; they are unified, simple, pure, unchanging, indivisible, and eternal.

The seat of these *Ideas* is first to be sought in the Good itself—that is, in God. They are distinguished only by the ground of their determination <note>their specific purpose or definition</note>; and so, while they are indeed distinct from one another, they are entirely of the same essence in their nature, for otherwise God Himself, as their author, would have to be changeable. Furthermore, one finds them in the spiritual world or the **World Soul** <term>World Soul: In Neoplatonism, the "Anima Mundi," an ethereal spirit that connects the physical world to the divine</term> as specific forms that are distinct from one another, so that while they are only one in God, they are manifold in the World Soul. They also dwell in souls, whether they are still united with the body or have been released from it. In nature, one finds them in the form of seeds, and finally in matter itself as shadows.

In the World Soul lie just as many *seminal causes* <note>original: "Seminalursachen"; from the Latin *rationes seminales*, these are the "blueprints" or spiritual germs from which all physical things grow</note> of things as there are *Ideas* in the divine mind; and by virtue of these causes, the stars and their configurations have received their existence and the properties belonging to them. And these friendships or enmities are strengthened or diminished according to the favorable or adverse position in which they find themselves. Now, just as these celestial bodies behave toward one another in the upper world <note>the Macrocosm or the heavens</note>, so do the things subordinate to them behave in the lower world <note>the Microcosm or the Earth</note>. The reason for this antipathy and sympathy lies simply in the desire to attract that which is of a similar nature or pleasant, and to flee everything that is of a contrary kind. Thus, certain animals have a natural affection for one another, and this is very often confirmed even among humans. But whether the reason for this is to be found precisely in a friendly and similar constellation of the stars, I shall leave in its proper place <note>an idiomatic expression meaning "I will leave that undecided for now"</note>.

# §. 5.

## Which Things are Subject to the Sun, the Moon, and the Remaining Planets.

In general, it is difficult to determine exactly which planet or other star a specific thing is subject to; for the most part, this rests upon conjecture derived from the imitation of the rays, the motion, and the shape, as well as from the smell, the colors, and occasionally also from an effect similar to those of the stars. Thus, to the **Sun** are attributed fire and flame; among the bodily fluids <note>original: "Säften"; literally "juices," referring to the classical humors or fluids of the body.</note>, the purest blood and the vital spirit; and in regard to taste, the sweet-sour; among metals, gold; among stones, the chrysolite, the hyacinth <note>In historical lapidaries, "hyacinth" often referred to a yellow, orange, or red zircon or garnet.</note>, the ruby, topaz, and chrysoprase; among minerals <note>original: "Minen"; referring to materials extracted from mines.</note>, orpiment <term>orpiment (Auripigment): A deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy.</term>; among plants, shrubs, and trees, all those that turn toward the sun, such as the sunflower, and those that close their leaves at the setting of the sun but open them again at its rising, like the lotus; also belonging under the government of the sun are celandine, the citron tree, pennyroyal, gentian, ginger, and vervain, the laurel tree, the cedar, the palm tree, the ash, ivy, and the grapevine, as well as mastic, saffron, balsam, ambergris <note>original: "Umbra"; here likely referring to "Ambra" or ambergris, a precious substance used in perfumery.</note>, musk, yellow honey, aloe wood, cinnamon, pepper, spearmint, cloves, marjoram, rosemary, and frankincense. Water, for example, corresponds with the earth by virtue of coldness, but with the air by virtue of moisture; the air with fire by virtue of heat, and fire itself with the heavens by virtue of its matter. In the same way, the soul unites with the body by means of the spirit, and the intellect <note>original: *Verstand*; the higher rational or divine faculty of the mind</note> with the spirit by means of the soul. 

The human body, according to its preparation, is thus the medium through which the spirit is attracted from above; and this spirit is then the foundation of the intellect and the soul, just as the dryness of wood is ready to absorb resin or oil, by which it afterward becomes the foundation of fire, and fire itself becomes the vehicle of light. The first image of God is the world, the image of the world is man, the image or imprint of man is the animal, and so forth. In this way, that which is above is connected with that which is below through similarity, and the influence flows from the highest beginning to the lowest link, like a stretched string that, when touched, immediately vibrates throughout and produces resonances. 

By means of this doctrine, the **magicians** <term>Magicians: Here referring to practitioners of "natural magic," a Renaissance and Enlightenment-era science that sought to understand and utilize the hidden laws and harmonies of nature.</term> sought to attract invisible and hidden forces through visible and tangible things. This occurred partly through the influence of the stars, through incense, lights, sounds, and other natural things that have some relationship with the heavenly, and which—besides their physical properties—also contain a certain incorporeal measure, number, and weight <note>original: "Maas, Zahl und Gewicht"; a common theological and alchemical reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20, implying that the universe is ordered by divine mathematical laws.</note> of hidden forces. 

This science of attracting the higher by means of the lower was extended by the ancients even to the heavenly spirits, whom they claimed to be able to make favorable and to summon by means of a fortunate constellation and other good preparations. The same could occur with evil spirits according to this doctrine; however, their summoning could only be [accomplished] through evil and loathsome things—

# On the Magic of the Ancients.

For this reason, the ancient diviners made use of incense—partly to attune the human mind, and partly to prepare a person to receive certain higher inspirations.

An innumerable multitude of things—whose smoke is said to produce many kinds of strange effects, such as summoning spirits or driving them away, obtaining the spirit of prophecy, seeing spirits, gathering animals in one place or driving them away, stirring up storms, and so forth—are passed over here for the sake of brevity.

### On Auguries and Divination.

A certain kind of divination <term>Wahrsagerey: The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means.</term> arises from natural causes and is confirmed through art and experience. Such were the auguries <term>Augurien: In ancient Rome, the practice of interpreting omens from the behavior of birds or other natural signs to determine divine will.</term> of the ancients; and there were many kinds of these. For some were taken from four-legged animals, some from birds, some from celestial things like thunder and lightning, some from falling objects—as when, for example, something fell in a temple—others were derived from sacrifices; and among these, some were of ill omen, such as if the sacrificial animal ran away from the altar, or cried out during the sacrifice, or even fell on the wrong side of its body.

Michael Scot <note>original: "Michel Skot"; referring to the 13th-century Scottish mathematician and scholar known for his studies in astrology, alchemy, and the occult.</note> lists twelve types of auguries, six of which were taken from the right side and six from the left. For instance, it was considered a good sign if one left the house early and encountered a person or a bird that afterwards settled to one's left. The other eleven types are of the same nature and significance. Divination was also performed using sneezing, because it was claimed to originate in a sacred place—namely the head, as the seat of the spirit. Likewise, the first speech a person uttered in the morning was regarded as an omen. Among all forms of divination, that from the flight of certain birds was most highly esteemed. Therefore, certain species of them were called "birds of omen," <note>original: "Vorbedeutungsvögel"</note> and their flight and movements were diligently observed. These were...

# Chapter Four.

## §. 1.

### **On the Resurrection of the Dead, Long Sleep, Abstinence from Food and Drink, and the Interpretation of Dreams.**

The ancients claimed that a human being can give their spirit such an impetus that it can transcend all sensory impressions, overcome them, and thereby attain the perfection of celestial spirits even while still here on earth. It was therefore no wonder that the idea eventually arose that one person could raise another from the dead through the power of their spirit. For, they said, since the human soul is immortal, all other spirits must obey the soul of a perfected individual; and consequently, a perfected person could, through the power and strength of their spirit, call back to life other less-perfect souls that had already been separated from their bodies. However, this miraculous power <term>Wunderkraft</term> <note>A German term for a supernatural or "wonder-working" power.</note> was not attributed to the strength of the spirit alone, but also required the use of certain herbs and other magical practices. Numerous examples of such resurrected individuals can be found in the writings of the ancients,

...which, however, all bear the mark of superstition and ignorance. Some [thinkers] have even arrived at the idea that those who were resurrected might not have been entirely dead, but rather had only lain in a long, deep faint <term>Ohnmacht</term> <note>A state of unconsciousness or swooning often mistaken for death in the pre-modern era due to lack of detectable pulse or breath.</note>, from which they were revived by the smoke of certain herbs and other known remedies; and thus it was later claimed that they had been raised from the dead.

Such resurrections occurred in ancient times perhaps just as frequently as in more modern ones. For there are states in certain illnesses, or even mere accidents, where the soul seems so completely separated from its body—deprived of all movement, sensation, and all life—that one might consider the person dead based on outward appearance. Sad experience has confirmed that such a state can last for several days, as people who lay in such a death-like faint, and who later came to themselves, have been buried alive.

It was presumably from this state—which is more similar to death than to sleep—that the adventurous stories arose concerning people who are said to have slept for a long time, even for many years consecutively. However, these stories all belong to the realm of the chimera <note>original: "Reich der Chimäre" – a reference to mythological delusions or impossible fantasies.</note>. For although someone might occasionally sleep for several days in a row after great exhaustion without waking and without taking nourishment, it is contrary to all probability and experience that a person could sleep through fifty-seven years without interruption, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and natural philosopher who recorded many such legends in his *Natural History*.</note> tells of a traveling boy.

-># Chapter Four.<-

We now come to the interpretation of dreams, or the art of exploring the future through them, a practice held in high regard by the ancient philosophers and theologians. Before all else, an actual dream—if it is to signify anything—must not be confused with those images that occur to one during a light slumber or during interrupted sleep; for these are of no significance and commonly stem from the impressions one had while in a waking state. For that which was pleasant or unpleasant to the mind <note>original: "Gemüth" – a German term encompassing the heart, mind, and emotional soul.</note> while awake usually continues to act during sleep, producing dreams that relate to it. 

The actual, meaningful dream is that which is impressed by celestial influences upon a person who is healthy in both body and spirit. The rules of interpretation are found among the astrologers; however, they are very uncertain and fluctuating because the impressions differ according to the physical and mental constitution of each individual, and thus no universally applicable rules can be given. In general, it was merely asserted that if one dreams often and repeatedly of one and the same thing, that which one dreams will come to pass. Therefore, says Aristotle <note>A reference to the Greek philosopher's treatises on sleep and dreaming, such as *On Prophesying by Dreams*, where he examined the natural rather than divine causes of dreams.</note>, one should diligently pay attention to dreams and their outcomes.

## § 2.

### On Visions, Inspirations, and Divination in the Waking State.

The mind sometimes detaches itself from all other sensory impressions while in a waking state and, as **Aristotle** <note>The author likely refers to the Peripatetic tradition or works like "On Prophesying by Dreams," though here Aristotle is cited to support the physiological basis of "ecstasy."</note> says, enters into a certain kind of **prophetic ecstasy**. One is then "outside of oneself," believing one sees and hears things that are not present, and the spirit seems, as it were, to have forgotten its body in such moments. This state is said to be particularly characteristic of people with a **melancholic temperament**; for they grasp and retain things quickly and intensely, their imagination is fiery, and thus it identifies very easily with the impressions received from above. The basis of this ecstatic state lies, therefore, in the melancholic temperament—yet not in that which from **black bile** <note>original: "schwarze Galle" — In the ancient theory of the four humors, black bile was the substance responsible for the melancholic temperament. # On the Magic of the Ancients.

And this they explained in a threefold manner; namely, according to the **imagination**, according to **reason**, and according to the **mind** <note>original: "Gemüth" — in this context, it refers to the highest faculty of the soul, distinct from mere logic or sensory imagination.</note>. 

Therefore, when the soul is stirred by **melancholy**, it tears through all bonds and obstacles that the body places in its way, transforms itself entirely into the **imagination**, and suddenly soars into the dwellings of the lower spirits, where it assumes many wonderful properties. There it learns to predict the effects of the elements, the change of seasons, rain, storms, earthquakes, famine, and so forth. 

If, however, it turns toward **reason**, it gains communion with the middle spirits and learns from them the science of all natural and human things. 

If, on the contrary, it turns toward the **mind**, it soars to the higher orders of spirits and receives the knowledge of future things, the recognition of the laws of God, knowledge of the order of angels, and everything that belongs to the science of the soul and its future state. 

These three explanations are very mystical; however, by omitting the cooperation of spirits, they can be explained much more naturally through the strength of the human spirit—namely, if one excludes future things and the spirit world, for the exploration of which we have no key, and which must therefore necessarily be explained through the mediation of spirits.

->§ 3.<-

### On the passions of the soul and their effect on the body; on the power of the imagination and its effect on other people; on the power of certain words, etc.

According to the concepts of the ancients, passions <note>original: "Leidenschaften" — intense emotions, drives, or "sufferings" of the soul.</note> are nothing other than movements or inclinations of the soul toward certain things that it considers either good or bad. They were divided into the sensory, the intellectual, and the spiritual. The sensory passions concern temporal good or evil, convenience or inconvenience, the pleasant or the disagreeable, and can be called natural or animal passions. However, if they arise from the intellect, they relate to good or evil with respect to virtue or vice, praise or shame, utility or harm, and are therefore called rational or voluntary passions. The spiritual ones, on the other hand, relate to good and evil with respect to right or wrong, the true and the false, and so forth. The basis of the passions lies in the soul's **faculty of desire** <term>faculty of desire: (German: *Begehrungskraft*) a philosophical term for the soul's capacity to be moved toward or away from an object of perception.</term>;

The attractive relates to absolute good or evil, and from this arises **love**, and in contrast, **hate**. The repulsive power of the soul relates to the good or evil in regard to the difficulties of attaining it, or the distancing and turning away from it. In this way, one finds eleven passions in the soul, namely: love, hate, desire, abhorrence, joy, pain, hope, despair, courage, fear, and anger. # On the Magic of the Ancients.

Therefore, they endeavored to explain the origin and essence of all things through the configuration of the Hebrew letters—their form, simplicity, composition, separation, curvature, straightness, lack, abundance, size, smallness, opening, closure, order, transposition, and so forth—applying this to both the letters themselves and their points <note>referring to vowel markings or "niqqud" which provide the "spirit" or sound to the "body" of the consonants</note>.

They divided the alphabet itself into three sections: namely, twelve simple letters, seven double letters, and three "mothers" <note>In the *Sefer Yetzirah* (The Book of Formation), the "Mother" letters are Aleph, Mem, and Shin; the "Double" letters have two pronunciations; and the "Simple" letters have one</note>. According to their astrological notions, these represented the twelve signs of the zodiac, the seven planets, and the three elements of water, fire, and earth; for they did not count air as a separate element, viewing it instead as the bond that connects the other three.

The accents and points took the place of astrological aspects <note>the specific angular relationships between planets that determine their influence</note>; and thus, the letters were seen as the sacred expression of higher powers, and every name composed from them was of great significance in magic. All other languages and scripts were thought to fall short of the Hebrew in expression and power, except for those original words that still retained their true meanings; all other words, being arbitrarily invented and assigned to things, were considered to be without power. The twenty-two letters of the Hebrews were held to be the foundation of the entire creation, from which the names and actions of all creatures, and indeed everything created, flows. Whoever devotes himself to this study must occupy himself with the composition and sequencing of these letters until the voice of God and the true sense of the holy text is revealed to him. # Fourth Chapter. 89

How arbitrarily people proceeded in this matter is clear from the division of the Greek and Latin alphabets. Since both of these languages have more letters than Hebrew, the "Air" and the "World-spirit" <note>often referred to as the *Anima Mundi*, a vital force thought to permeate all nature</note> had to be included in the Greek count, so that the former could be accepted as an element. 

In the Latin alphabet, on the other hand, seven vowels were assumed for the sake of the seven planets—namely, A, E, I, O, U, Y, and V <note>The author notes that V and U are counted as distinct letters here to reach the sacred number seven, despite their shared history in Latin script</note>. The remaining consonants, with the exception of H, designated the twelve signs of the Zodiac; H, however, represented the World-spirit. Because of this inconsistency and confusion, these latter two languages were presumably declared to be less effective <note>referring to their perceived lack of "magical potency" compared to the "divine" Hebrew</note>. 

The letters themselves possessed a double numerical significance: first, a simple one according to their sequence as they appear in the alphabet; and second, a collective one, whereby each letter was assigned the sum of all those preceding it <note>This describes a cumulative system of numerology where, for example, the third letter represents the sum of 1+2+3</note>. Finally, there were certain "integral numbers" derived from the names of the letters themselves. Through the knowledge of the powers of these numbers, it was believed that the deepest mysteries, as well as the future, could be explored—of which more will now follow.

Upon them rests the transformation of the elements, the change of seasons, the course of the stars, and the movement of the universe; everything exists through numbers. # Chapter Five.

->§. 1.<-

## Concerning Numbers and Their Effects, as well as Geometrical Figures.

Above all, it must be noted that when numbers are spoken of in magic, one should by no means understand them as sensory, material, or so-called commercial numbers; for these were declared completely ineffective by the Pythagoreans <term>Pythagoreans: followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who taught that the universe is governed by mathematical proportions and that numbers possess mystical properties</term>. Instead, one understands by them a certain quantity of forces, forms, and proportions attributed to them, just as, in a physical sense, geometrical figures serve to define a certain space. This knowledge of numbers and their inner meaning is the key to all the mysteries of the ancients and, as they say, the most direct path to prophecy. Everything, they say, that exists is determined by a certain number, measure, and weight <note>This is a reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "But thou hast arranged all things by measure and number and weight." This concept was used by ancient and medieval scholars to bridge the gap between religion and science.</note> according to its internal essence and external form; and numbers are the archetype <term>Urbild: a primordial model or spiritual blueprint from which all physical things are derived</term> of all things created. Upon them rest the change of the elements, the turning of the seasons, the course of the stars, and the movement of the universe; everything exists through numbers. Chapter Five.

The more unmixed and simple a substance is, the more it approaches its origin, and the more effective its powers become. The ancients founded the edifice of their sciences upon this doctrine; and not only the knowledge of natural things and their effects, but also the supernatural, the unknown—in a word, the entire spirit world—rests upon the theory of numbers <term>Zahlenlehre: literally "number-lore," referring to the mystical or occult study of numbers, often called arithmology</term>. In the expression of the ancients, they are the sacraments of God and nature. The Pythagoreans <term>Pythagoreans: followers of Pythagoras who believed that "all is number" and that mathematics held the key to the cosmos</term> were particularly in possession of this science. However, since little or nothing complete of their actual teaching has come down to us—as they covered it with the thickest veil of secrets and propagated it among themselves only orally <note>This refers to the "Pythagorean Silence," a vow of secrecy taken by initiates to prevent the "profane" from learning their sacred mathematical truths</note>—nothing remains to us of this but mere fragments and conjectures. In general, the following classification of numbers occurred: simple units signify divine things, tens signify heavenly things, hundreds signify earthly things, and thousands signify those things yet to come. A multitude of meanings were attributed to numbers derived from Holy Scripture, but we do not wish to dwell on their account here, as we have resolved to treat the Pythagorean theory of numbers separately in the following discourse. There is also a diversity of opinion among the ancients regarding number theory itself, which is all the more inexplicable because no reason for it can be discerned, and all evidence is lacking. We come, therefore, to the application of numbers to letters, and the resulting <term>divination: the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</term>; and thus follows

He divided the circles of the elements in the same way: to Fire, he gave the planets and the Dawn; to Air, the thundering Jupiter and Juno; to Water, Oceanus and Thetis; and to Earth, Pluto and Proserpina. ## Chapter Six.

->Section 1.<-

->On the disposition of the mind in which a<-
->magician should find himself; on silence<-
->and purification.<-

We now come to the higher part of magic, or to that which contains the religious duties and prescriptions. Here and there in the preceding sections, something has already been said about the purification of the body and the soul, which everyone who wishes to achieve anything in this science <note>original: "Wissenschaft" – in this historical context, it refers to a systematic study of the occult or spiritual arts rather than modern physical science.</note> must undertake. This was very strictly observed, and above all, it was insisted that everyone who wished to undertake anything of this kind must have a healthy body, free from all diseases, and a calm and content soul, undisturbed by passions. Furthermore, he had to be a zealous and genuine worshiper of God, without any hypocrisy; for only through true and heartfelt piety can one make oneself pleasing to God and receive something from Him. Such a person, inwardly convinced of the Deity and truly pious, the ancients said, would be as much elevated above his fellow brothers as God Himself is elevated above the angels. In every performance, one must appear pure in body and soul, surrendering oneself entirely to the grace and goodwill of the Deity,

and then, with the senses entirely withdrawn, offer his sacrifice, and with a calm mind await the outcome, and praise and invoke the super-celestial <term>Bacchus</term> <note>original: "Bachus" — here referring to the Orphic or mystical aspect of the deity associated with spiritual rebirth and the "divine frenzy."</note> as the author of renewal, from whom so many streams of divine power flow into our hearts. This was most strictly forbidden by <term>Pythagoras</term>, <term>Plato</term>, and all their followers; and <term>Orpheus</term> demanded a fearsome oath from those he initiated, that they should reveal nothing of the secrets of religion to the uninitiated. We now proceed further to the three main pillars of religion, through which we can attain knowledge of the truth and which are indispensable in magic: these are Love, Faith, and Hope. Love is the strongest bond of the soul, the most excellent of all things; it has its origin in heaven, from where it descends into the heart of man and fills his countenance with heavenly beauty; it maintains and nourishes hope and provides the strength for execution. Hope, when it is unchangeably directed toward that which it desires, and is not made wavering or restless by any doubt, nourishes and strengthens the mind <term>original: "Gemüth" — the seat of human soul, temperament, and emotional character</term> toward all that is good.

Fauns, Satyrs, Pans, Nymphs, Naiads, Nereids, Dryads, Pierides, Hamadryads, Castalides, Muses, Graces, Lemures <note>original: "Lemuren" — in Roman mythology, these were the wandering and vengeful spirits of the dead.</note>, Genii, and so forth, who are held to be gods by the common people, but by others to be demigods. This third class of demons is, according to Plato's opinion, as numerous as the stars in the heaven. The number of good demons is said to exceed all conception; and as a contrast, there is likewise an immense number of impure spirits in the underworld. After these follow the spirits of darkness or of malice, the **fallen angels**. These are called evil demons; and their number is also said to be very large. They are also divided according to the cardinal directions, stars, and elements, and have their kings, princes, and overseers, as well as their names. Among them are four regents according to the four cardinal directions, who again have a multitude of others under them who command the legions. From this arose the Gorgons and Furies of the ancients, as well as the Hound of Hell <note>A reference to Cerberus, the multi-headed dog that guarded the gates of the underworld.</note>. According to the opinion of more recent theologians, the whole world of angels is divided into three classes, and each class again into three divisions; so that in total **nine orders** emerge.

## On the Magic of the Ancients.

Those among the ancients <note>Referring to classical philosophers or early Gnostic thinkers who speculated on the soul's descent</note> who held this view believed that the evil spirits, who yearned to return to the light, were first placed into a fleshly body where they had to endure their period of trial. In this manner, the human race as a whole was thought to have descended from the fallen angels. But we shall not dwell on this point, and instead move on to another no less singular opinion: namely, that concerning the bodies of demons.

This is a subject of great dispute among theologians. Some asserted that angels, as well as all evil spirits, possessed no bodies at all, though they could occasionally assume a form which they would soon after discard. Others maintained that they were strictly incorporeal <note>meaning existing entirely without physical or material substance</note>. **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), an influential Christian philosopher</note>, on the other hand, says in his commentary on the first book of **Moses** <note>The Book of Genesis</note> that demons possess bodies of air or fire which are not dissolved by death, because the active element <note>In ancient and medieval physics, fire and air were considered "active" elements that moved and transformed, while earth and water were "passive" or "suffering" elements</note> within them holds the upper hand over the passive one. 

He adds further that from the beginning of creation, all angels were clothed in bodies consisting of the purest air, which were very well-suited for action but not for suffering. Those who remained in goodness kept these bodies; the renegades, however, received in their place bodies of coarser and thicker air, so that they could also be tormented by fire. The opinions on this matter are so confused, and at times so absurd, that one must be astonished at how people could argue over things about which we know absolutely nothing. It was therefore no wonder that, where there is no foundation and no insight, one lost oneself in sheer absurdities,

# On the Magic of the Ancients.

...whether a person has only one such protector or several around them, opinions on the matter are divided. On the whole, the only consensus is that all people are governed by good spirits and are guided to that degree of virtue of which they are worthy; but those who have renounced virtue are increasingly provoked and seduced by evil demons, until they finally reach the reward for their evil actions—namely, the utmost degree of misery. 

However, those people who are governed by higher angels are also preferred above other men; for the angels lead and guide them, and subject other people to them through a certain secret power, so that everyone feels their own insignificance in their presence, cannot deny them their respect and reverence, and fears them everywhere. Regarding the manner in which one can learn about the protective spirit assigned to each person, the ancients have written many fables. It all rests on the doctrine that in every part of the world there are certain angels and spirits who are more powerful in that region than in others, and thus also exert a stronger influence on the people living there.

### §. 5.

#### Of the Names of the Angels and Spirits, and their Calling or <term>Summoning</term> <note>original: "Citation." From the Latin *citatio*, referring to the formal ritual of calling a spirit to appear.</note>.

The actual names of the angels and spirits, as well as those of the stars, are completely unknown to us, and we can never recognize them without closer divine revelation. However, one still finds some traces of them in the Holy Scriptures; and the Hebrews therefore believed that Adam bestowed names upon all creatures, as well as upon the spirits, according to the well-known verse in the <term>First Book of Moses</term> <note>The Book of Genesis, specifically chapter 2, verses 19-20.</note>, Chapter 2. Thus, the idea arose that man could bestow certain effective names upon the spirits; yet this could only be done by one who is already equipped with divine power. But since it is nevertheless impossible to find a name in human language that would correspond to the divine nature or the essence of the angels, certain names have been bestowed upon them according to their **functions**, which signify certain effects that one expects from them. These names take, in a sense, the place of sacrifices and venerations, and are said, according to the assertion of the ancients, to have great power in magic. One also finds enough examples in the ancient writings of names which, written on paper or **parchment**, are said to have produced a strange effect; but they all fall too much into the superstitious to be able to cite any of them here.

# On the Magic of the Ancients.

Substance, indivisible, present in all parts of the body, and so arranged by the Creator that its essence depends on its active power, but by no means on its material body; it is a <term>substantial number</term> <note>In ancient philosophy, particularly Pythagorean and Platonic thought, a "number" was considered a fundamental, living principle that gives structure and order to reality.</note>, uniform, equal to itself, and raised far above all materiality, and its power does not stem from matter or from lower earthly things, but from the First Cause. Viewed as a number, it is independent of all physical laws; therefore, it can neither be divided nor doubled. # On the Magic of the Ancients.

<meta>catchword: the</meta>

We now wish to touch upon something regarding the state of man after death: and here it is first to be known that the ancients divided man into **spirit**, **soul**, and **body**; and regarding this they held the following opinions: The **spirit** comes from God or from the world of spirits, and is therefore immortal and eternal; the **soul** or **reason**, however, comes from the stars and enjoys a long duration; the **body**, by contrast, arisen from matter, is subject to destruction and corruption. Consequently, the soul is immortal through the spirit; by virtue of its <term>ethereal vehicle</term> <note>The "ethereal vehicle" (or *ochema*) is a concept from Neoplatonic and Hermetic philosophy describing a subtle, "star-stuff" body that carries the soul through the heavens and into the physical body.</note> it has a long duration; but if it is not surrounded by a new body once again, it is nonetheless dissolvable. It is thus only immortal insofar as it is united with an immortal spirit. However, not all men, says **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian-Greek sage to whom the *Hermetica*—foundational texts of Western alchemy and magic—are attributed.</note>, receive such a living spirit, because it is designated by God as a prize or reward, as it were, for the soul. Now, those who neglect their soul do not receive it, and remain, like the animals, under the dominion of the senses. As soon as the body ceases, and its parts are dissolved into vapors, such a soul disappears like a shadow and has no part in immortality. Regarding the fate of these three, the **Hebrews** believed that the body, immediately after death, fell into the power of the demon **Zazel** <note>In occult systems like that of Agrippa, Zazel is the spirit associated with the planet Saturn. Here, the author links him to the decay of the physical form.</note>, who is also called the lord of flesh and blood*; in whose power it remained until it was purified, sanctified, and reconciled. From this arose the offerings for the dead of the ancients, which

Now it remains to mention something of the manner in which it was believed the dead could be summoned. It is clear from what has been said thus far that certain souls still retain a strong inclination toward their abandoned bodies after death. Such souls, whose bodies still lie unburied or in desolate places, as well as those who were forced to leave their bodies through a violent death, wander around them just as they would around a dear friend or relative. And of these it was claimed that if one knows their favorite inclinations, which they once harbored while in their bodies, and furthermore employs certain scents that were once pleasant to them and other things, they could easily be summoned. Sacred lights, sounds, invocations, and everything by which the soul can be stimulated must not be neglected in this process. The poets therefore said that one could summon the souls of the deceased by means of their corpse and their blood, to which other things such as milk, oil, honey, wine, flour, and the like were added; however, this would only be possible in such places where these souls had formerly preferred to stay, and were still drawn to even now by a certain, as it were, irresistible inclination; furthermore, also in places intended for the punishment and purification of souls, known through apparitions and other visions, such as churchyards, places of execution <term>Hochgerichte: Historically, these were sites of "High Justice" where capital punishment was carried out, often featuring permanent gallows or scaffolds</term>, battlefields, where the bodies of the slain still lie unappeased and unburied. The cooperation of evil spirits, wandering about for their penance, is likewise required for this; and the **sorcerer** forces them, by means of the methods known to him, to carry out his will.

## §. 7.

### On Inspiration, the Rapture of Ecstasy, Prophetic Dreams, and how a True Magician must Prepare themselves Inwardly and Outwardly.

Inspiration occurs, according to the opinion of the **Platonists** <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato, who in this context likely refers to the Neoplatonists who merged Greek philosophy with mysticism</note>, by means of the union of the gods or the higher spirits with our souls; and this union arises through a certain attraction of the same, which is difficult to explain, and of which one can only say that it has its basis in a firm, invincible faith. Through this, man attains the gift of predicting the future and delivering **oracles** <term>Orakelsprüche; divine pronouncements or prophecies</term>. To maintain these inspirations, however, it is necessary that the soul in such moments be completely free from all foreign thoughts and not be distracted by any other object. This state was divided by the ancients into three categories:

# Sixth Chapter.

...divided, namely into *inspiration*, ecstasy, and prophetic dreams. A brief description of each shall now follow here. *Inspiration* itself was further divided into four sub-sections. The first was *inspiration* from the *Muses*. Through this, the mind is elevated and made capable of attracting forces from above through the powers of natural things. Under the name of the *Muses*, the ancients understood the souls of the heavenly *spheres* <note>In classical and medieval cosmology, the universe was seen as a series of nested "spheres" surrounding the Earth, each associated with a planet or celestial body</note>. The lowest of these *spheres* belongs to the *Moon*; and under its dominion stands the entire vegetable and mineral kingdoms; and to this belongs everything that can be prepared from these things in a magical manner, such as *talismans*, *amulets* <note>original: "Anhängsel"</note>, *ointments*, and so on; and so it continues to ascend. The second *sphere* belongs to *Mercury*, the third to *Venus*, the fourth to the *Sun*, the fifth to *Mars*, the sixth to *Jupiter*, the seventh to *Saturn*, the eighth to the *starry firmament* <note>original: "Fixsternenhimmel"; the sphere of the fixed stars beyond the planets</note>, and the ninth to the *cause* of the *first motion* <term>Primum Mobile; the outermost moving sphere in classical astronomy which was believed to drive the motion of all the inner spheres</term>.

The second kind of *inspiration* is that of *Dionysus* <note>original: "Dionysio"</note>. One prepares for this through internal and external purifications, *exorcisms*, *sacraments*, festivities, and holy rites. Through these, the soul is tuned to high contemplations and becomes receptive to the divine spirit, which fills it with happiness, wisdom, and knowledge of the future through its promptings—not indeed through certain signs, marks, or conjectures, but by means of a certain voluntary stirring or *modification* of the mind. The third kind of *inspiration* is that of *Apollo*, and occurs through holy mysteries, vows, and invocations,

### Chapter Six. 155

Ecstasy <term>Entzückung: a state of being "carried away" or outside oneself; from the Greek 'ekstasis'</term> consists in a separation, removal, and enlightenment of the soul, through which it is guided from lower objects to the contemplation of higher ones. This state arises through a sustained preoccupation with the most sublime subjects, so that the soul, as it were, completely immerses itself in them. Through constant wishing and fervent desire, it unites itself entirely with the highest wisdom and, as Plato says, turns away so much from all sensory and bodily things that it seems at times to have completely abandoned them, leaving the body behind without motion.

The human soul, it was claimed, has such great power—if it remains true to its essence and is not governed by the force of the senses—that it can suddenly and quickly soar into the supracelestial regions, both within and outside the body. There, it is enlightened by God, as the source of all wisdom, and is equipped with the knowledge of hidden things. Therefore, Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, often cited by Renaissance and Enlightenment writers as a source of "primeval wisdom."</note> says:

->You must ascend to the light itself and to the rays of the Father, from whence you received your soul;<-

and Pythagoras in his golden sayings:

Knowledge of himself. He spoke with the spirits while his body continued walking, and he arrived at the place where he wanted to go without losing his way and without becoming weary. If someone was about to die, he saw the funeral procession passing through the streets several days before their death and exhorted those who were around him to make way!!! <note>original: "A. d. H." — Editor’s Note. This anecdotal section likely refers to a specific historical figure or "clairvoyant," possibly Emanuel Swedenborg, whose abilities were often described in these terms during the 18th century.</note>

To this also belongs the opinion of the Egyptians, who held that the soul contained a certain spiritual light within itself and, when it is released from the body, fills all places and times, and is lacking nowhere because it is always and everywhere present. Now, when a person or a soul has reached this highest degree of the most perfect contemplation <term>Beschauung: a state of deep spiritual beholding or mystical meditation</term>, it is pulled away from all created particulars and then recognizes—not piecemeal, but through ideal intuition—the ideal light itself with a single glance. Of this light, Plato says, only extremely few people would partake in this life; and according to his opinion, not even all the gods could attain it. 

There is also a certain kind of ecstasy <term>Entzückung: a state of being "carried away" or outside oneself</term> that holds the middle ground, so to speak, between supernatural divination and natural prophecy. This arises through overwrought passions, such as from insurmountable love or sadness, or also in the agony of death at the end of life, in which state future things can sometimes be predicted. The explanation for this is as follows: there lies within our soul a certain great power capable of encompassing everything, which is, however, obscured by the darkness of the body and hindered in its effects, but after death it regains its freedom and perfect knowledge. It is for this reason that dying or elderly people are sometimes quite unusually enlightened and think more clearly, because their soul is then less fettered by the senses, and the bonds that unite them with the body have, as it were, already slackened. Thus, at the crossroads of life and death, they can easily receive revelations that appear to them mingled with the pangs of death. 

We come now to the third kind of divination <term>Weissagung: the act of foretelling or prophecy</term>, or to prophetic dreams: these arise through the imagination <term>Einbildungskraft: the creative power of the mind to form images</term> and through the understanding, or also through a higher enlightenment of our soul, or through direct revelation. Whoever wishes to receive such dreams must first and foremost keep their mind <term>Gemüth: the inner soul, disposition, or emotional state</term> pure, unblemished, and free from all cares, so that it may be receptive to all spiritual impressions and can capture the higher rays like a polished mirror. 

When the body is healthy and the mind is calm, when we have burdened ourselves with neither food nor drink, nor are oppressed by want, and furthermore when neither anger nor lust rules over us, and we then lie down to sleep—it is then that the soul is in the best state to receive and reflect the higher rays. For this, a calm, steady, and religious mindset <term>Denkungsart: a philosophical or spiritual way of thinking</term> is also required.

# On the Magic of the Ancients.

Not a single dream, the ancients claimed, was entirely without meaning, but rather always carried something real within itself; and every dream would come to fulfillment <term>Erfüllung: the realization or coming true of a prediction</term> at the latest after the passage of twenty-two years. What they based this opinion upon is uncertain, and no explanation can be found regarding this. The preparations for a prophetic <term>prophetisch: relating to foretelling the future</term> dream consist of the following: the body must be healthy, the head free from all vapors <note>historical medical term referring to internal gases or "humors" believed to cloud the mind</note>, and the soul free from all unrest. On the same day that one wishes to receive the dream, one must abstain from eating and drink only as much as is absolutely necessary; the bed must be white and clean, the room consecrated and fumigated <note>likely with incense or herbs</note>, and the sleeper should place certain rings upon their fingers and lay holy images beneath their head. Thus should they lie down and fix their thoughts firmly upon that which they wish to know; and then, through the dream, they will receive the most desirable and truest revelations.

We come now to the preparations which, according to the concepts of the ancients, everyone who wishes to achieve anything in magic <term>Magie: the art of influencing events through supernatural means</term> must undertake both internally and externally. It has already been stated repeatedly that purity of the mind <term>Gemüth: the inner soul or emotional disposition</term> and of the body, good morals, and a pious conduct of life <term>Lebenswandel: the way one lives and behaves</term> are the most excellent and necessary requirements for this. Everything that approaches animal nature and clings to the flesh—just as rust clings to iron—places obstacles in the path of the true magician <term>Magier: a practitioner of the ancient, sacred arts of hidden knowledge</term>, because it disturbs the serenity and peace of the soul and directs it toward lower objects. ## Chapter Six.

The <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>From the Greek for "naked philosophers," these were ancient Indian ascetics who practiced extreme renunciation and lived without clothing to show their detachment from worldly needs</note> were required to wash three times during the day and twice during the night before they were permitted to enter the temple; they also made use of white linen garments which were washed daily. Regarding this, the following passage is found in <term>Hesiod</term> <note>An ancient Greek poet, roughly a contemporary of Homer, whose works often detailed the proper religious conduct of daily life</note>:

> No one dares to pour out wine to Jupiter at dawn with unwashed hands, nor to any of the other immortals; they do not wish to hear such people, and they reject their prayers. <note>original: "Nemo sub aurora Ioui audet fundere vina / Illotis manibus, sed et immortalibus vllis, / Non sic exaudire volunt, spernuntque precati."</note>

and in another place he says:

> Whenever a wicked man crosses a river with unwashed hands, the gods are enraged with him, and grant him sorrows thereafter. <note>original: "Prauus vbi fluuium manibus non lotis obiuit, / Huic Dii succensent, tribuentes inde Dolores."</note>

In this regard, it should also be noted that when a sacrifice was made to the upper gods, the entire body had to be purified by washing; however, if the invocation was intended for the gods of the underworld, a mere sprinkling with water was sufficient. Through abstinence, man is protected against all promptings of evil spirits and is consecrated as a temple of God. Moreover, it is highly necessary for the preservation of the body's health to observe the strictest moderation in food and drink, and to consume only what is necessary to maintain health and the cheerfulness of the spirit at all times. To achieve this end, all dried foods, frequent washing, rubbing <note>referring to ritual massage or friction to stimulate the skin</note>, physical exercise, and the greatest cleanliness in clothing and other things are useful, as are incense offerings, through which the spirit is encouraged and refined. For this reason, the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>The priestly and scholarly caste of India, renowned in European occult literature for their ancient wisdom</note> admitted no one to their mysteries who did not abstain from wine, meat, and

The most effective means of attaining this is undoubtedly solitude. Amidst the bustle of the world, the throng of business, and the pressure of worries, it is impossible to gain such mastery over oneself. The wisest men of antiquity therefore lived mostly in solitary places, or at least retired to solitude from time to time, in order to abandon themselves to their reflections and to enjoy the communion with themselves in quiet peace. Thus, according to the opinion of the ancients, *Zoroaster* <note>The ancient Persian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism, who in Western occult tradition was often viewed as the father of magic.</note> lived in solitude for twenty-two years; and *Orpheus* <note>A legendary Greek hero, musician, and poet; he was considered a primary source of sacred knowledge and mystical rites.</note> stayed for a long time in the Thracian deserts. *Pythagoras* is said to have lived in hiding for ten years; and it is well known of *Democritus* and *Heraclitus* <note>Two influential pre-Socratic Greek philosophers; Heraclitus was famously known as the "Weeping Philosopher" for his solitary and melancholic nature.</note> that they lived gladly and almost always in solitude. It would be superfluous, however, to further elaborate here on the advantages that solitude grants the spirit, as we have recently received one of the most excellent works on this subject*. The most important part of the <term>Doctrine of Purification</term> <note>original: "Reinigungslehre"—referring to the philosophical and mystical process of cleansing the soul of earthly attachments to prepare it for divine insight.</note>, however, consists of repentance and improvement. This must occur voluntarily. For, as *Seneca* says (in his tragedy *Thyestes*), he who repents of an evil deed is half innocent <note>original: "wer eine böse That bereut, ist halb unschuldig" / Latin: "Quem poenitet peccasse paene est innocens."</note>. It is the most effective among all means of reconciliation, and consists not only in the repenting of evil deeds, but in the total surrender and submission to the will of God and the firm longing to live according to His commandments. Everything evil, therefore, that comes from the mouth and the heart, must be entirely cast off and rooted out. The ancients, however—

The practice was as follows: in the same city or place where the plague reigned, the most shameful person <term>pharmakos</term> <note>A "pharmakos" was a human scapegoat used in Ancient Greek rituals to provide a "cure" for a city's misfortunes.</note> was sought out, seized, and led to the site with cakes and dry figs in hand. Among the Egyptians, one counted six hundred and six different types of sacrifices, which were offered to the planets as well as to individual stars. For they claimed that their spirit rested upon the sacred animals, and that they consequently must be invoked, and that they heard the prayers directed to them and granted gifts. To every planet and star, one sacrificed—as has been mentioned several times—using the animals, herbs, etc., proper to it. The observation and proclamation of these holy and unlucky days belonged to the duties of the priests, and they had to ensure that on the former <note>referring to the holy or festival days</note> nothing unholy was undertaken, such as bloodshed, death sentences, and the like.
