# Notice.

The famous author had, in the preparation of
this fable, the intention to draft the plan and description
of a college in which the greatness and
variety of the works of nature are explained,
and therefore called it the **Salomon’s House** <note>original: "Salomonische Haus." Also known in English as "Solomon’s House," it represents a visionary research institution.</note>, or
the **College of the Six Days’ Works** <note>original: "Kollegium der sechs Tagwerke." This refers to the biblical creation narrative, suggesting that the college's work is a continuation of divine creation through the study of nature.</note>; he has, however,
left it unfinished. The plan itself, in the manner of
poets, turned out larger and far more comprehensive than it
perhaps could have been carried out in reality *;
nevertheless, in many parts it is worthy of
human diligence.

---

* Mr. Nicolai <note>Friedrich Nicolai (1733–1811), an influential German Enlightenment writer and bookseller.</note> says of this in his *Essay on the Accusations made against the Order of the Templars* <note>original: "Versuch über die Beschuldigungen, welche dem Tempelorden gemacht worden." Nicolai attempted to link the origins of Freemasonry to the Templars and Bacon's ideas.</note>,
Part 1, pages 187 and 188: “This novel, decorated with all the
fictions and colors as they were in accordance with the taste of
the time, contributed perhaps

We set sail from Peru <note>In the 17th century, Peru was a key hub of the Spanish Empire; setting the departure here emphasizes the vastness of the Pacific exploration to follow.</note>, where we had stayed for a full year, and intended to take our course toward China and Japan. The provisions we had with us were sufficient for twelve months; and so we sailed for five months and more with a favorable, though weak and intermittent, east wind. But then the wind turned and blew steadily from the west for many days in a row, so that we made only very slow progress, and at times even thought of turning back. Afterward, however, a violent and stormy south wind arose with some inclination toward the east, which was as much as possible against us and drove us toward the north; and at this time our provisions, although we managed them very sparingly, were almost entirely exhausted. Seeing ourselves now almost abandoned in the middle of the vast ocean and without provisions, we considered ourselves lost and expected nothing but death. We, however, lifted our hearts and voices to the Creator of heaven, who shows his wonders even in the depths <note>A reference to Psalm 107, often cited by sailors in the early modern period.</note>, and implored his grace that, just as he in the beginning of things gathered the waters and brought forth the dry land

Windows, some of which were made of glass while others were of fine linen soaked in oil <note>In the 17th and 18th centuries, glass was expensive and often reserved for the wealthy; oiled linen was a common, practical alternative that allowed light to pass through while providing protection from the elements.</note>, gave the building a great elegance. Our answer was: the total number, of both the healthy and the sick, amounted to fifty-one people, among whom were seventeen sick. He then asked us to wait for a while until he would return to us; and this happened after about an hour. Then he showed us the beds that had been prepared for us, nineteen in number. It seemed they had calculated so that four of these beds, which stood somewhat apart from the rest, were intended for the four most distinguished among us, each of whom was to sleep alone; in the remaining fifteen, however, they were to sleep two by two. The beds themselves were very neat and extremely clean. Then he led us into a long corridor, which was very similar to a monks' dormitory <note>original: "Mönchsdormitorium." This corridor, which contained eighty cells—and thus far more than we needed—was intended for the use of the sick; and our guide also told us that as soon as one of our sick recovered, he could be moved from the cell into a bed, for which purpose ten others were ready beyond the number mentioned before. The king of this island at that time, named **Altabin**, who was a very wise man and an experienced general, knew both the strength of the enemies and his own quite accurately. He arranged matters so that their troops, after they had landed, were cut off from their fleet; and so he surrounded the army and the fleet with a greater force than they possessed, so that they were forced to surrender without a battle. Once they were in his power, he imposed no harsher conditions upon them than that they must swear never to bear arms against him again in the future; and so he let them return unharmed. 

Soon afterward, however, divine vengeance punished this audacious undertaking within a period of approximately one hundred years. For the great **Atlantis** <note>Referring to the American continent.</note> was almost entirely devastated and destroyed—not by earthquakes, as your author <note>Plato, whose dialogues *Timaeus* and *Critias* are the primary sources for the Atlantis legend.</note> claims, for earthquakes are not so dangerous in these regions, but rather by a flood. Even today, those regions have larger rivers and higher mountains from which the water can pour into the plains than any part of the old world <note>Europe, Asia, and Africa.</note>. 

The flood, however, was not very deep, and in some places the water rose no higher than eighty feet. Thus it happened that, although the humans and animals in the lowlands were drowned, the wild inhabitants of the mountains were nevertheless able to save themselves. Nineteen hundred years ago, a king reigned over this island whose memory is sacred to us. We revere him not in a superstitious manner, but as a mortal man whom the Divinity used as an instrument. His name was **Solamona**, and we regard him as the lawgiver <note>In the original German "Gesetzgeber," referring to a founder of a legal system, much like Lycurgus or Solon of Greek history.</note> of this people; his heart was pure goodness and truth, and his entire concern was directed toward making his land and his people happy. 

When he considered that this land was productive enough to sustain itself through its own strength without foreign help—since it is sixteen hundred miles in circumference, the largest part of which is very fertile and of good quality—and furthermore reflected that the ships of the empire could be sufficiently occupied with transport from one port to another and to neighboring islands; and when he considered the flourishing prosperity in which the land found itself at that time, and realized that every change or innovation could lead to a thousandfold worsening, but never to further improvement: he believed he had to crown his work by seeking—as much as is possible for human wisdom—to secure and make permanent for all time the happy state in which the country then existed, in order to achieve his great and noble purpose. Among his fundamental laws, one of the foremost and most important was therefore this: that the entrance to this land should remain closed to all foreigners, whose arrival among us at that time (namely after the misfortune <note>Referring to the great flood mentioned on the previous page.</note> that had struck **America**) was not uncommon.

This law stemmed from the fact that he expected nothing good from innovations and the mingling of customs. A similar prohibition regarding the entry of foreigners did indeed prevail among the ancient Chinese, and is still practiced among them today; however, it is not respected there, and only makes the people curious, inexperienced, fearful, and clumsy. Our lawgiver, on the other hand, took entirely different considerations into account when drafting this prohibition: for first, he secured the rights of humanity through his foundations and ordinances for the benefit of poor travelers, which you yourselves have experienced.

At these words, we all stood up and bowed, whereupon he continued: Since this king wanted to unite the duty of philanthropy <note>The German term "Menschenliebe" (love of humanity) reflects the utopian ideal of balancing state security with universal moral obligations.</note> with politics, but it seemed to him entirely contrary to this duty to keep foreigners away by force—while on the other hand, it could harm our state if they returned and spread the secrets of this island—he chose the following middle path: He decreed that foreigners who landed here should not be refused if they wished to return; however, to those who wished to stay, a certain status and way of life should be assigned by the state, and the necessary support for it would be provided. A few days later, I made the acquaintance of a merchant of the same city, whose name was Joabin. He was a Jew, and circumcised. For there were a few Jewish tribes present there who had free exercise of religion; and they could have obtained this permission all the more easily since the customs of these Jews were very different from those of the Jews in the rest of the world. For while other Jews detest the name of Christ and harbor a secret, deep-seated malice against the nations among whom they live, these instead revere our Savior to the highest degree and love the people of Bensalem as their brothers. This man of whom I speak admitted that Christ was born of a virgin and lived as a most excellent man; afterwards, God had chosen him to be the Prince of the Seraphim <note>The highest rank of angels in traditional celestial hierarchies, said to be closest to God's throne.</note> who stand before His throne. ### Editor’s Preliminary Report

Initially, I intended to publish this work only in extract form, inserting my own remarks into the text here and there. However, since I realized later how important its content is for the historical researcher, and that it contains much that can serve to clarify a history so shrouded in darkness as that of the <term>Brotherhood of the Rosicrucians<note>The Rosicrucians were a secret society of mystics and alchemists whose existence became a major intellectual sensation in Europe during the early 17th century.</note></term>, I decided to provide a faithful translation of it. Only this one thing must I note: that I have omitted some superfluous matters here—for example, the dedication, in which (beyond the author’s intention to oppose the palpable lies of darkness with the sun of truth) nothing further is contained than a compliment to the State Councilor of Genegault. I also believed I could omit some insignificant French and Latin poems—with the exception of the one by Menapius <note>Menapius was a pseudonym used by writers involved in the early Rosicrucian controversies; the editor chooses to keep this specific poem while discarding others deemed less relevant.</note>—which appear at the beginning of the original. In all other respects, however, everything has remained as it was in the original manuscript itself. 

As proof of the rarity of this little work, one may cite what Mr. Nicolai <note>Friedrich Nicolai (1733–1811) was a famous Berlin bookseller and writer of the Enlightenment who investigated the history of secret societies.</note> says on page 187 of the second part of his *Essay on the <term>Knights Templar<note>The Knights Templar were a medieval military order; Nicolai’s work sought to find historical links between the Templars, Freemasons, and Rosicrucians.</note></term>*: "after much inquiry, he had not yet been able to 'lay eyes upon it.'" I encountered it, after much futile searching, in the Erfurt University Library.

<margin>* Naudé was a Parisian; and it is this city that is meant here.</margin>

I frankly confess to you, dear reader, that I have never been so at odds with myself, nor found myself in such an embarrassment, as that in which I have been for several days. On one hand, nature obliges me to take a compassionate interest in the misfortune of this flourishing city* and to seek to alleviate its distress, as it was only recently afflicted by a contagious disease; yet now it is being unsettled by the poison of a false and ridiculous opinion, which certain idle men seek to instill into the imaginations of her dearest sons in order to confuse their understanding and undermine the good opinion held of their wisdom. On the other hand, however, ignorance struggles against my good will, and does not permit me to draw as much benefit from my studies as would be necessary to combat such a chimera <note>The German "Hirngespinnst" literally means a "brain-spinning," referring to a wild fantasy or delusion.</note> and erroneous opinion. By doing so, I believe I can settle the matter by way of negation, proving that all these fabulous tales have always been harmful and detrimental to those who believed in them.

This is, I believe, all that can be expected on such a subject. Like a giant bound within a single link of a chain, or the entire world depicted on a small globe, this matter is condensed into the ten chapters of this report. This should be particularly pleasing to the reader, for within the space of just a few sheets, he can find with little effort everything that he could only extract with great difficulty from the writings of all those who have written before me. Furthermore, **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work *De Medicina*.</note> speaks for me when he says: *when knowledge is equal, a friendly physician is nonetheless more useful than a stranger* <note>original Latin: "cum par Scientia sit, tamen vtiliorem Medicum esse amicum quam extraneum"</note>.

## Chapter One.

### On the Inclination of the French to Adopt All Sorts of New and Ridiculous Opinions.

Phlegon of Tralles <note>A Greek writer and freedman of the Emperor Hadrian, active in the 2nd century AD.</note>, a freedman of the Emperor Hadrian, once wrote from Egypt in the name of his master to a distinguished Roman senator who had three times held the honor of the consulship. He began his letter with a judgment of that country in the following manner: "Egypt, which you praise to me, Servianus; I have found it to be entirely fickle, unstable, and fluttering at every breath of rumor." <note>original Latin: "Aegyptum quam mihi laudas Serviane; totam didici leuem, pendulam et ad omnia famae momenta volitantem."</note> I hope to be forgiven if, by applying this passage to my countrymen to criticize their actions, I seem at the very beginning of this treatise to accuse them of fickleness <note>original: "Leichtsinn"—implying a lack of serious reflection or a tendency toward frivolous changeability.</note>. However, I am not the first to make this reproach against them, nor the first to wish to see somewhat more restraint in their behavior. Julius Caesar already noted in his *Commentaries* <note>Refers to Caesar's "Gallic War," where he frequently comments on the temperament of the people he encountered.</note> that the ancient Gauls, their ancestors, were accustomed to stationing themselves in crowds along the paths of strangers and travelers, even forcing merchants to tell them news from the lands they had just come from, so that from this information they might "enter into deliberations on the highest matters; of which they necessarily had to repent immediately, since most people gave them fictional answers according to their wishes." <note>original Latin: "de summis rebus consilia inirent; quorum eos e vestigio poenitere necesse erat, quuum plerique ad voluntatem eorum ficta responderent."</note>

To be sure, one will object to me here that even **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) who argued that all humans by nature desire to know.</note> considers it a pleasant and entertaining occupation when one uses their time to learn something, especially when the object of our knowledge—through its novelty, peculiarity, and variety—incites us to a more perfect understanding of it. ## Chapter Two.

### That the silliest opinions have always found followers.

An old opinion, which I formerly held to be true and elevated above common human sense, was this: that just as politicians assert that no one seeks to preserve his freedom <note>original: *Freyheit*</note> at the risk of his life without eventually attaining it, so too could one say of the learned that fortune has favored only a few great minds. ### True History of the Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross.

In my opinion, however, nature could only have received this power from the great Creator of heaven, who accomplished the two greatest secrets of His divinity through a single word, and thus willed that what He created from very little should follow His example in the production of all creatures. ### Regarding the Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross

[They swore] to faithfully and inviolably keep the [statutes] he had left behind for them, which consisted of the following:

To practice the art of medicine <term>Arzneykunst: the practice of medicine and the preparation of remedies</term> voluntarily and free of charge.

Everyone shall dress according to the fashion of the country in which they reside.

Everyone shall present themselves at the Congregation once a year.

Everyone shall look for a skilled and suitable successor <term>Successor: a chosen heir to the brother's knowledge and place in the order</term> who is capable of representing him and filling his place.

The sign R. C. shall be the symbol and hallmark of the Brotherhood.

If one of them should die in a foreign land, the place of his burial shall remain hidden.

The Congregation shall be kept secret for 120 years; and the brothers should firmly believe that, if this society were to suffer destruction anywhere, it could nevertheless be completely restored at the tomb of its first founder <note>The "Stifter" or founder refers to the legendary Christian Rosenkreuz.</note>.

Although all these statutes were very easy to observe, they nonetheless flattered themselves that by observing them, they would receive such invaluable favors and privileges from God as have never yet been granted to any creature. # Message to France

One of the primary whims <note>German: "Grillen," meaning caprices or eccentric notions.</note> of **Philipp Bombast Aureolus Theophrastus Paracelsus**, who was a native of Switzerland and wished to distinguish himself as much by the multitude of his names as by the novelty of his harmful teachings, was this: that he wished to persuade us he was the forerunner of a certain **Elias the Artist** <note>original: "Elias Artista." A legendary messianic figure in alchemy predicted by Paracelsus to reveal all secrets of the art at the end of time.</note>, who would come after him, enlighten the world, and possess the true secret of the transformation of metals and all other sciences, in order to eradicate the corruption that has come into the world through the length of time. "That which is more useful," he says in the eighth chapter of his book on minerals, "God allows to be revealed; but that which is of greater importance" <note>original: "Quod vtilius est, Deus patefieri sinit, quod autem maioris momenti est"</note>—namely the transformation of base metals into gold—"remains hidden from the common people until the arrival of Elias the Artist, when he shall come" <note>original: "vulgo adhuc latet vsque ad Eliae Artistae aduentum, quando is venerit."</note>. Likewise, in the first treatise of the same book, he says the following: "This item is true: there is nothing hidden that shall not be revealed; therefore after me shall come one whose greatness <note>original: "magnale." A Paracelsian term for a great work or essence.</note> does not yet live, who shall reveal many things" <note>original: "Hoc item verum est, nihil est absconditum quod non sit retegendum, ideo post me veniet cuius magnale nondum viuit, qui multa reuelabit."</note>. And these passages were accepted as pure truth by **Alexander von Suchten** <note>The text spells it "Schuten." **Postel** <note>Guillaume Postel (1510–1581), a French polymath and visionary who sought to unify all religions.</note>, who was too proud to want to owe anything to others, brought his mother **Johanna** <note>Mother Johanna, or the "Venetian Virgin," whom Postel believed was the spiritual "Mother of the World."</note> onto the stage when he saw that Paracelsus had established an **Elias**. He claimed that she was to fulfill the secrets of religion during the general renewal of all things. all those points in time in which something remarkable and excellent has occurred. This whim <note>original German: *Grille*</note> will ultimately be found just as false as that of **Arnold of Villanova** <note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, who, according to the report of **Pico della Mirandola**, announced to us the appearance of the **Antichrist** for the year 1345; furthermore, that of **Albumasar** <note>An influential 9th-century Persian astrologer.</note>, who set the duration of the Christian religion until the year 1440; that of an **Abraham**, who announced the arrival of the **Messiah** to the Jews for the year 1464; and all the other **astrologers** who prophesied a general **Great Flood** for the year 1524. Furthermore, the prophecy of a **Cyprian Leovitius** <note>A Bohemian astronomer and astrologer (1524–1574).</note>, who had calculated ephemerides <note>Tables of the positions of celestial bodies.</note> for thirty years beyond the end of the world; and those of **Savonarola** <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498), a Dominican friar and preacher in Renaissance Florence who claimed prophetic visions.</note>, which were daily refuted by the excellent conduct of the **Dukes of Tuscany**, and which he made known so often in **Florence** at the instigation of **Soderini**.

> I have likewise publicly preached, and again affirm by divine inspiration, that whatever Florentine citizen shall endeavor, at home or abroad, to usurp the sovereignty in that city for himself, or to violate the newest form of government, God will severely punish him together with his whole house and all those conspiring with him, and finally bring him to perish by a pitiable end. <note>original Latin: "Item palam praedicaui, rursusque affirmo, ex diuina Inspiratione, quod quisquis ciuis Florentinus domi forisue procurabit principatum sibi in ea ciuitate usurpare, aut nouissimum regimen violare, cum uniuersa domo sua cunctisque secum conspirantibus, eum Deus grauiter puniet, ac demum lacrymabili exitu faciet interire."</note>

# Message to France

...as well as the tales of **Guillaume Postel** <note>A French visionary and polymath (1510–1581) who claimed an elderly woman named Johanna was the "Mother of the World."</note> regarding his Mother Johanna—all of which, taken together, have been refuted and proven false by **Time**, the father and avenger of truth. This can serve as a guide for us to determine our judgment of the **Elias** of **Paracelsus**, who is nothing more than a creature of his own imagination, and thus deserves far less belief than the aforementioned astrologers who at least cite the whole of **astrology** to prove their promises and prophecies.

Rather, we can answer this even more decisively if we accept what **Penotus** <note>Bernard Georges Penot (c. 1519–1617), a physician and alchemist who became a critic of Paracelsian methods.</note> says in his work, *On the Medical Denarius* <note>original Latin: *de Denario medico*</note>, namely: that Paracelsus compiled several of his writings and treatises from the works of **Lanfranc of Milan**, **Arnold of Villanova**, **Raymond Lull**, **Rupescissa**, **Harland**, and **Trithemius**. Furthermore, it is claimed he appropriated the works of a German monk who, according to the report of **Crato** <note>Johannes Crato von Krafftheim (1519–1585), a prominent imperial physician.</note>, wrote on <term>chemistry<note>The original "Chymie" here refers to alchemy and early chemical medicine.</note></term> two hundred years before him; or, as **Melchior Adam** <note>A 17th-century biographer of scholars.</note> reports, those of a famous chemist named **Isaac Holland** <note>Isaac Hollandus, a legendary Dutch alchemist whose works were highly influential but of uncertain date.</note>, who wrote in German and whose writings Paracelsus published under his own name.

Since he perhaps foresaw that, in time, the works of Isaac Holland would be published and his own would be suppressed by the discovery of such an obvious fraud, he used a ruse to persuade us that after him a certain **Elias Artista** would come and teach us all the secrets clearly and plainly—the very secrets he had hidden within the labyrinth of his writings under obscure phrases and newly invented words. "This man," <note>original Latin: *Hic*</note> says Penotus, "is Isaac Holland himself..." <note>original Latin: *ipse Isaacus Hollandus*</note>

For since they claim to know everything, it follows that they must also know this secret. The best way to judge the present is undoubtedly to recall the past, and to judge the outcome of the former by that of the latter. However, when we consider the great list of impostors that Coras <note>Jean de Coras (1515–1572), a French jurist famous for his account of the case of Martin Guerre, a celebrated 16th-century case of identity theft and imposture.</note> presents in his history of Arnauld <note>Arnauld du Tilh, the man who famously impersonated the soldier Martin Guerre.</note>, and the tales of a certain Sebastian of Portugal <note>Sebastian I (1554–1578), the King of Portugal who vanished in battle. By this means they hoped to deceive those who, like the citizens of the city of Rhinocolura <note>An ancient desert city where criminals were sent after having their noses cut off. The author is using a play on words: these "noseless" citizens lack the "scent" or discernment to sniff out a fraud.</note>, showed that they had no nose to recognize them, especially since Saint Jerome also says (in his *Letter to Nepotian*): *nothing is so easy as to deceive the common and unlearned people with a glib tongue, for they admire whatever they do not understand.* <note>original Latin: "nihil est tam facile, quam vilem plebem et indoctam, volubilitate linguae decipere, quae quidquid non intelligit admiratur."</note> The author of all these lies was also so cunning as to persuade us in the preface of the *Reformation* <note>Likely the *Refformation der Wolffart* (The Reformation of the Whole Wide World), one of the primary Rosicrucian manifestos.</note> that a certain Adam

Haselmeyer <note>Adam Haslmayr (c. 1560–1630) was a Paracelsian scholar and the first person to publicly mention the Rosicrucian manifestos. This too has occurred, and I find in a small pamphlet of three or four sheets a tale of a certain pilgrim or traveler who appeared in a German city around the year 1615. Acting as a physician, he predicted the death of a certain woman whom he had previously had under his care. He claimed to understand many languages and boasted of a knowledge of the secret effects of simple remedies. From time to time, he recounted events that had occurred in the city during the period he was staying there. In a word—excepting his medical art, in which he possessed some skill—he was the perfect likeness of the Wandering Jew <note>The "Wandering Jew" is a mythical figure from European folklore, a man cursed to walk the earth until the Second Coming; here he is used as a trope for a mysterious, eternal-seeming traveler.</note> described for us by Cayet <note>Pierre-Victor Palma-Cayet (1525–1610), a French historian. Molterus therefore laid this story before the world for judgment, in order to learn whether it could provide proof of the legitimacy of this society.

# Report to France

...it is an easy thing to chatter about quintessence <note>The "fifth element," believed by alchemists to be the purest essence of a substance.</note>, the universal medicine <note>A hypothetical "cure-all" substance, often equated with the Philosopher’s Stone.</note>, the philosopher’s stone, the signature of things <note>The *Signatura Rerum*, a theory that the outward appearance of objects reveals their inner spiritual purpose or medicinal use.</note>, treasures, planets, intelligences <note>In the occult traditions of the time, "intelligences" were the spiritual beings or angels believed to govern the movements and influences of the planets.</note>, magic, Kabbalah <note>A form of Jewish mysticism that was widely adopted and adapted by Christian scholars and occultists during the Renaissance.</note>, chemistry <note>The original German *Chymie* referred to a blend of what we now call chemistry and alchemy.</note>, and other secret things before a troop of ignorant rabble, who are accustomed to admiring everything they do not understand; or even in the presence of those who could indeed respond, if they were not deprived of the freedom to do so by those encyclopedic oracles, who cannot bear any contradiction in their assertions. I can only view these oracles as diligent and melancholy pedants who are swept away by a desire for the most secret things, just as those who, after reading *Amadis* <note>*Amadis de Gaula*, a famous chivalric romance; the author is comparing Rosicrucians to people whose minds are warped by reading too many fantasy novels, much like Don Quixote.</note> and similar romances, are ready to expose themselves to all dangers. Consequently, they make it a point of honor to imitate Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often cited by occultists.</note> as the god of all their follies, consider themselves Rosicrucians, and finally, by virtue of their wild and melancholy temperament, are forced to flee into the most lonely and remote wildernesses.

Pico della Mirandola will likewise refuse, as a second Alexander, to involve himself with these thieves and robbers who daily plunder his works to fill their own writings, which they wish to commend to us through that "divine light" which we, as philosophers—and so as not to involve ourselves in confusion—leave to the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism.</note>, Rabbis, Theologians, and Talmudists <note>Scholars of the Talmud, the body of Jewish civil and ceremonial law.</note>

## Chapter Nine.

### Inconsistencies found within the principles of this
### society and in the *Amphitheater* of Khunrath,
### along with an explanation of the latter.

If it is true that in a creature as perfect as a woman is in the eyes of most men, one has nevertheless discovered one hundred and two faults—which, beyond those she shares with our own sex, are so entirely peculiar to her that, according to the observation of <term>Alvarus Pelagius: Alvaro Pelayo (c. 1280–1352), a Franciscan bishop and influential canon lawyer</term> in his book **On the Lament of the Church** <note>original: "de Planctu Ecclesiae"</note> (Book 2, Chapter 45), one rarely finds a woman free of them; then I have no doubt that if one took the trouble to closely examine the **Fama** and **Confessio** <note>The *Fama Fraternitatis* (1614) and *Confessio Fraternitatis* (1615), the two primary manifestos that announced the existence of the secret Rosicrucian order to Europe.</note>, through which this high Brotherhood first made itself known to us, one would very easily discover therein several thousand errors, fantasies, lies, impossibilities, contradictions, and other fallacies. The Jesuit, Father Robert <note>Jean Robert (1569–1643), a Jesuit who wrote against the "magnetic" cures and alchemical theories of the era.</note>, has pointed out several of these in the 17th section of his **Goclenius, the Self-Tormentor** <note>original: "Goclenius Heavtontimorumenos." It is a great error to believe that philosophy consists merely in knowing how to explain a passage of Aristotle <note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), the foundational Greek philosopher whose works dominated medieval and early modern academic curricula.</note> from the lecturer’s chair or in a student's home. The Jew Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> thoroughly refutes this opinion when he says in the *Life of Moses*: philosophy consists of three things, namely plans, speech, and actions, all of which aim at a single purpose: the promotion of happiness. This true philosophy teaches us that we should produce no word that does not agree with our true mindset, and it forbids us from accepting every new legend as truth. This is so that France cannot be accused of having received and nourished such ridiculous and absurd opinions, and so that the French * do not lose the respect they have earned among foreigners for their prudence by approving and believing in a matter that, in every respect, can only bring them shame.

We also command that the fortune-tellers <note>original: "Wahrsager"</note>, who pretend to be inspired by God, shall be chased out of the land, so that good morals are not corrupted by the hope for vain future things, or the minds <note>original: "Gemüther"</note> of the people led astray. # Appendix
## of several
### Rosicrucian Statutes.*

->The six articles of the *Fama*.<note>The *Fama Fraternitatis Rosae Crucis*, published in 1614, was the first manifesto of the Rosicrucian Order, outlining its history and rules.</note><-

->1.)<-

No brother shall practice any other profession than curing the sick, and that entirely for free.

2.) No one shall be forced to wear a specific dress on account of the Brotherhood, but rather should follow the custom of the country.

3.) Every brother shall appear every year on Day C <note>Scholars generally interpret "Day C" as a reference to a specific secret meeting date, often associated with the "House of the Holy Spirit."</note> at the *Holy Spirit* <note>original: "S. Spiritus"</note>, or send the reason for his absence.

4.) Every brother shall look for a capable person who might succeed <note>original: "succediren"</note> him in the event of his death.

5.) The letters *R. C.* shall be their seal, watchword, and character.

6.) The Brotherhood shall remain secret for one hundred years.

---

\* I am attaching this appendix of statutes here, partly because it will be more pleasant for the reader to be able to read them here as a whole, but also partly to make it easier to compare to what extent the original statutes were deviated from. <note>original: "A. d. H." — Anmerkung des Herausgebers, or Editor's Note.</note>

## Five Articles,
### upon which the Knights of the Golden Stone in the Chymical Wedding swear. <note>These oaths appear in "The Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz" (1616), an allegorical romance and foundational Rosicrucian text attributed to Johann Valentin Andreae.</note>

1.) You, Sir Knights, shall swear that you will at all times attribute your Order to no devil or spirit, but to God alone, your Creator, and His handmaid, Nature.

2.) That you will hold all whoredom, unchastity, and impurity in hatred, and not stain your Order with such vices.

3.) That you will come to the aid of all people <note>original: "männiglich"</note> who are worthy and in need of your gifts.

4.) That you do not desire to use such honor for worldly splendor and high standing.

5.) That you do not wish to live longer than God wills.

---

## Special Articles.
### How a disciple <note>original: "Discipulus"</note> of celestial magic <note>original: "Magiae coelestis"</note> should conduct himself in regard to himself, toward God, as well as toward his preceptor <note>original: "Praeceptorem" — a teacher or tutor</note> and toward other people.

->(From Sperber’s *Echo of the Fraternity*, printed in Danzig 1616.) <note>Julius Sperber was a prominent early defender of the Rosicrucian movement; his work *Echo der Fraternität* sought to link the brotherhood to ancient mystical traditions.</note><-

1.) He shall be God-fearing.

2.) He shall observe the discipline.

3.) He shall have no special involvement with the world.

4.) He shall be pious, pure, and blameless.

5.) He shall be sober and moderate.

This congregation of ours was previously established by our ancient heroes with very strict clauses and laws, through which our new Brotherhood perceived that this alone was the reason why so few of them are found now; therefore, around the year 1624, they issued their decree and voice throughout the whole world to summon the brothers, of whom only nine of them and two apprentices were found. N." as a placeholder for the initiate's name.</note> promise to the eternal and living God, that I shall reveal the secret which has been communicated to me by you (afterward he raises two fingers) <note>A traditional gesture for swearing a formal oath.</note> to no single human being, but rather to keep the same sealed within me with the natural seal <note>A metaphorical reference to the initiate's own lips or mouth.</note> for the duration of my life; as also regarding its effects, as far as I shall be aware of them, which have been taught to me by you through written revelation <note>Secret knowledge or instructions delivered in writing.</note> or by your instruction, not to reveal the slightest thing, nor to discover anything of the state of our brotherhood, neither the location, nor the name and surname of the Emperor, nor to show the Stone <note>Refers to the Philosopher’s Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> to anyone; and regarding all this, I promise to maintain an eternal silence even at the risk of my life, so help me [God], etc.

Then his teacher <note>original: *Lehrmeister*</note> comes and cuts off seven tufts of his hair, seals them in seven small pieces of paper, writes the brother’s name and surname upon them, and gives them to the Emperor.

<page-num>367</page-num>
<header>Statutes of certain Rosicrucians.</header>

...to keep safe. The following day, the brothers go to the new brother's quarters and dine together without speaking a single word or greeting one another.

When they depart, however, they shall say:

> Brother of the gold or of the rose, may God be with you in perpetual silence, as promised to God and to our holy Union; <note>original Latin: "Frater aureae vel roseae, Deus sit tecum cum perpetuo silentio, Deo promisso et nostrae sanctae Coniugationi;"</note>

and they shall do so for three consecutive days.

46.) When the three days have passed, they shall distribute a gift to the poor according to their own judgment and intention.

47.) They may remain together in one of our houses for two months, but no longer.

48.) During this time, the brothers shall become well-acquainted with the new brother and will be able to instruct and teach him as much as possible.

49.) The brothers are commanded to have no more than three ecstasies <note>In this context, "ecstasies" likely refers to specific ritual trances or meditative states induced during alchemical or spiritual work.</note> while they are in our great house, as these involve certain operations that belong solely to our Magistery <term>Magistery: The technical mastery or "Great Work" of alchemical and spiritual transformation.</term>, in order to draw more light into this mystery and so that everything remains concealed.

50.) When the brothers interact with one another, they shall call each other by the name given to them on the day of their profession <note>The formal "profession" of vows when officially entering the order.</note>.

<header>Appendix of some Rosicrucian Statutes.</header>

51.) However, in the presence of strangers <note>Individuals who are not initiated members of the brotherhood.</note>, they shall let themselves be called by their true baptismal and family names.

52.) A new brother shall always be given the name of the brother who most recently passed away. And so, the aforementioned rules shall be strictly observed by all brothers who have been admitted among us and have sworn the oath of faith in the name of our Lord J. C. <note>Jesus Christ.</note>.
